verses.text: Early in the morning, the chief priests, elders, scribes, and the whole Sanhedrin devised a plan. They bound Jesus, led Him away, and handed Him over to Pilate.
So Pilate questioned Him, "Are You the King of the Jews?" "You have said so," Jesus replied.
And the chief priests began to accuse Him of many things.
Then Pilate questioned Him again, "Have You no answer? Look how many charges they are bringing against You!"
But to Pilate's amazement, Jesus made no further reply.
Now it was Pilate's custom at the feast to release to the people a prisoner of their choosing.
And a man named Barabbas was imprisoned with the rebels who had committed murder during the insurrection.
So the crowd went up and began asking Pilate to keep his custom.
"Do you want me to release to you the King of the Jews?" Pilate asked.
For he knew it was out of envy that the chief priests had handed Jesus over.
But the chief priests stirred up the crowd to have him release Barabbas to them instead.
So Pilate asked them again, "What then do you want me to do with the One you call the King of the Jews?"
And they shouted back, "Crucify Him!"
"Why?" asked Pilate. "What evil has He done?" But they shouted all the louder, "Crucify Him!"
And wishing to satisfy the crowd, Pilate released Barabbas to them. But he had Jesus flogged, and handed Him over to be crucified.
Then the soldiers led Jesus away into the palace (that is, the Praetorium) and called the whole company together.
They dressed Him in a purple robe, twisted together a crown of thorns, and set it on His head.
And they began to salute Him: "Hail, King of the Jews!"
They kept striking His head with a staff and spitting on Him. And they knelt down and bowed before Him.
After they had mocked Him, they removed the purple robe and put His own clothes back on Him. Then they led Him out to crucify Him.
Now Simon of Cyrene, the father of Alexander and Rufus, was passing by on his way in from the country, and the soldiers forced him to carry the cross of Jesus.
They brought Jesus to a place called Golgotha, which means The Place of the Skull.
There they offered Him wine mixed with myrrh, but He did not take it.
And they crucified Him. They also divided His garments by casting lots to decide what each of them would take.
It was the third hour when they crucified Him.
And the charge inscribed against Him read: THE KING OF THE JEWS.
Along with Jesus, they crucified two robbers, one on His right and one on His left.
And those who passed by heaped abuse on Him, shaking their heads and saying, "Aha! You who are going to destroy the temple and rebuild it in three days,
come down from the cross and save Yourself!"
In the same way, the chief priests and scribes mocked Him among themselves, saying, "He saved others, but He cannot save Himself!
Let the Christ, the King of Israel, come down now from the cross, so that we may see and believe!" And even those who were crucified with Him berated Him.
From the sixth hour until the ninth hour darkness came over all the land.
At the ninth hour, Jesus cried out in a loud voice, "Eloi, Eloi, lema sabachthani?" which means, "My God, My God, why have You forsaken Me?"
When some of those standing nearby heard this, they said, "Behold, He is calling Elijah."
And someone ran and filled a sponge with sour wine. He put it on a reed and held it up for Jesus to drink, saying, "Leave Him alone. Let us see if Elijah comes to take Him down."
But Jesus let out a loud cry and breathed His last.
And the veil of the temple was torn in two from top to bottom.
When the centurion standing there in front of Jesus saw how He had breathed His last, he said, "Truly this man was the Son of God!"
And there were also women watching from a distance. Among them were Mary Magdalene, Mary the mother of James the younger and of Joses, and Salome.
These women had followed Jesus and ministered to Him while He was in Galilee, and there were many other women who had come up to Jerusalem with Him.
Now it was already evening. Since it was Preparation Day (that is, the day before the Sabbath),
Joseph of Arimathea, a prominent Council member who himself was waiting for the kingdom of God, boldly went to Pilate to ask for the body of Jesus.
Pilate was surprised to hear that Jesus was already dead, so he summoned the centurion to ask if this was so.
When Pilate had confirmed it with the centurion, he granted the body to Joseph.

So Joseph bought a linen cloth, took down the body of Jesus, wrapped it in the cloth, and placed it in a tomb that had been cut out of the rock. Then he rolled a stone against the entrance of the tomb.
Mary Magdalene and Mary the mother of Joseph saw where His body was placed.

context.author: Traditionally John Mark, a companion of Peter
context.genre: Narrative Gospel — the trial before Pilate, mockery, crucifixion, death, and burial, told with almost no editorial comment, letting the events themselves carry the weight
context.audience: Roman Christian readers, given an account of a Roman method of execution they would have understood all too well firsthand
context.setting: Jesus is tried before Pontius Pilate, Roman governor of Judea from AD 26-36, then taken to Golgotha — "the Place of the Skull" — traditionally identified with the site beneath the Church of the Holy Sepulchre, just outside the first-century city walls.
context.custom: Pilate's custom of releasing a prisoner at the feast isn't independently attested outside the Gospels, but fits a plausible pattern of Roman provincial governance aimed at keeping restless populations calm during high-tension festivals. Wine mixed with myrrh was commonly offered before crucifixion as a mild painkiller — Jesus refuses it, apparently choosing to face the full weight of what's coming with unclouded awareness.
context.timelineImmediate: This chapter covers roughly nine hours of a single day, from early-morning trial to a three-in-the-afternoon death and same-day burial, driven by the practical urgency of completing everything before the Sabbath began at sundown.
context.timelineBible: Jesus' cry "Eloi, Eloi, lema sabachthani" quotes Psalm 22:1 word for word, and the soldiers casting lots for His garments (v.24) fulfills Psalm 22:18 with striking precision — a psalm of suffering written roughly a thousand years earlier.
context.sparkNotes: Jesus is tried before Pilate, who finds no real fault in Him but hands Him over anyway to satisfy the crowd demanding Barabbas's release instead. Soldiers mock Him as a fake king, then crucify Him at Golgotha between two criminals — and at His death, the temple veil tears in two and a Roman centurion, of all people, declares, "Truly this man was the Son of God." Joseph of Arimathea, a member of the very council that condemned Him, boldly asks for His body and buries it before sundown.

translation.meaning: The Roman method of execution reserved largely for slaves, rebels, and the basest criminals — a deliberately shameful, public death.

translation.greek: Ἐλωῒ Ἐλωῒ λεμὰ σαβαχθανί (Elōi Elōi lema sabachthani)
translation.meaning: Aramaic, quoting Psalm 22:1 directly — "My God, My God, why have You forsaken Me?" — the only words from the cross Mark records.
The curtain separating the temple's Most Holy Place from the rest — its tearing "from top to bottom" pictures a barrier removed by God's own action, not torn from below by human hands.

occurrences.note: Hebrews later calls Jesus' own body this same word — "the veil, that is, His flesh" — tying His torn body directly to the temple veil torn at His death.

gospelParallels.note: Matthew's parallel account of the same trial, crucifixion, and burial.
Luke's version, which includes Jesus' words to the repentant criminal beside Him.
John's account, with additional detail on the dialogue between Jesus and Pilate.

otBackground.note: "My God, My God, why have You forsaken Me" — quoted word for word as Jesus' cry from the cross.
Soldiers casting lots for a sufferer's garments, written roughly a thousand years before the event it describes.
The suffering servant given "a grave with the rich" — echoed in Joseph of Arimathea's wealthy, honorable tomb.

commentary.note: Henry connects Jesus being bound directly to Psalm 118:27's language of sacrifices bound with cords — "Christ was bound, to make bonds easy to us." He also cites Cicero's own description of crucifixion, teterrimum supplicium, "a most tremendous punishment," noting Christ met death in its most extreme, deliberately shameful form — the death reserved for slaves and the worst criminals — and thereby conquered it.

On Pilate releasing Barabbas, Henry notes the irony sharply: Pilate released "the scandal and plague of their nation" while condemning "the glory and blessing of their nation" — not from conviction, but simply to keep the crowd quiet, "willing to content the people." Political expedience, not justice, decided who lived and who died that day.

Ryle calls Barabbas's release 'a vivid emblem of the manner in which God pardons and justifies the ungodly' — a guilty man walking free while an innocent one dies in his place, the exact shape of the exchange at the center of the gospel itself.

Lewis does not comment on Mark 15, but "The Perfect Penitent" in Mere Christianity is a reflection on what the cross is for. He says that the central Christian belief is that Christ's death put us right with God and gave us a fresh start, and that how it works is less important than the fact. The explanation he offers is that only God made human could submit and repent perfectly on our behalf. (Paraphrased; Lewis's works remain under copyright.)

overview.summary: At dawn Jesus is handed to Pilate, who releases Barabbas and has Jesus flogged. He is crucified at Golgotha, cries out in the words of Psalm 22, and dies. A centurion confesses, and Joseph of Arimathea buries Him.

history.t: Pilate governed Judea from AD 26 to 36 and was known for harshness.
Rome crucified rebels publicly to frighten others into obedience.

customs.t: Prisoners were beaten before crucifixion, often weakening them.
A written charge was fixed above the condemned person on the cross.

archaeology.t: A heel bone with an iron nail was found in a Jerusalem tomb of this era.
A stone from Caesarea names Pontius Pilate as prefect of Judea.

overview.discussion: A Roman centurion called Jesus the Son of God as He died. Why might that confession come from him?
